title: Happens-before and causal precedence
summary: Derive Lamport's happens-before relation from local order, send-before-receive, and transitivity.

sections.title: The partial-order relation
sections.body: Happens-before is generated by local program order, by a send event preceding its receive, and by transitive closure. It is a partial order: some pairs remain incomparable.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: The relation is the semantic foundation for FIFO, causal ordering, Lamport clocks, and vector timestamps.

reference.sourceId: L. Lamport, Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System

sections.title: Concurrency is incomparability
sections.body: Two events are concurrent when neither happens-before the other. Do not infer that concurrency is transitive: two adjacent incomparable pairs do not force the endpoints to be incomparable.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Exam traces often test the difference between 'not proven ordered' and a positive concurrency claim.

reference.sourceId: L. Lamport, Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System

examples.title: Prove or reject an order
steps: Check local order on one process.
Check whether a send matches a receive.
Apply transitivity only along established edges.
If neither direction is derivable, label the events concurrent.
examples.answer: A causal graph makes the proof auditable: every arrow needs one of the three rules.

contrastDrills.prompt: If neither event happens-before the other, how are the events classified?
contrastDrills.explanation: Concurrency means both directions of happens-before fail; it is a relation of incomparability.
contrastDrills.misconception: Name the ordering, time, or communication boundary before choosing.

math.latex: e \to f \iff (e\text{ precedes }f\text{ locally})\ \lor\ (e=\mathrm{send}(m),\ f=\mathrm{receive}(m))\ \lor\ (\exists g:\ e\to g\land g\to f)
math.explanation: The happens-before relation is generated by local program order and send-before-receive, then closed transitively. Two events are concurrent when neither direction can be derived.

symbols.meaning: message connecting a send to a receive

math.name: Happens-before relation
math.purpose: Use it to derive causal precedence from local order, communication, and transitivity.

math.latex: e_i^x \to e_j^y \Longleftrightarrow (i=j\land x<y)\ \lor\ \mathrm{send}(e_i^x)\prec\mathrm{receive}(e_j^y)\ \lor\ \exists e_k^z:\ e_i^x\to e_k^z\to e_j^y
math.explanation: The lecture's happens-before relation is generated by local process order, message send-before-receive, and transitive closure. It is a partial order, so some event pairs remain incomparable.
math.name: Indexed happens-before rule
math.purpose: Use it to derive causal order from local execution, message delivery, and transitive closure.

criticalQuestions.prompt: If $e_i^x\not\to e_j^y$, can you immediately conclude $e_i^x\parallel e_j^y$?
criticalQuestions.angle: Check both directions, not only one.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: No. Concurrency requires both $e_i^x\not\to e_j^y$ and $e_j^y\not\to e_i^x$.

criticalQuestions.angle: Trace a causal chain that crosses more than one message or process.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: An event can influence a later event indirectly through intermediate events; transitivity records that inherited dependency.
